content:
Joint owners initially denied entry; staff said only one person allowed in

From 9 am, residents gradually entered Tin Fai Community Hall, some arriving by tour bus. At around 10 am, when several joint owners tried to enter, staff demanded that only one person could go in, with another admitted only if seats were available. This provoked the owners' displeasure, who protested at the hall entrance: "Pulling all this nonsense… you've got so many venues… you've already done the maths," and "It's only a thousand-plus flats, why act so sneakily?"

When a reporter tried to film, police officers intervened and directed them to a press area outside the hall, saying no loitering or filming was allowed on site. On-site staff told owners that it had been clearly stated online that only one owner per unit could enter. However, checking the records, Hop On only said that due to venue capacity limits, each unit could only be represented by the owner or an authorised representative, without specifying a number limit. The affected owners were eventually all allowed in before the meeting started.

At Tin Fai Community Hall, some joint owners were initially refused entry when they tried to get in. Staff said venue constraints allowed only one person to enter, with another admitted only if seats were available, while those unable to enter queued up nearby.

Mr Mak of Wang Yan Court: Just a work report meeting, far from satisfactory

About two hours after the meeting began, following the first round of voting, at around 1 pm, a small number of residents left, including Mr and Mrs Mak, owners of a high-floor flat in Wang Yan Court, and several other residents. As one of the owners who had co-signed to convene the meeting, Mr Mak frankly admitted he had no expectations beforehand: "We just came to see how they'd run this so-called owners' meeting," and the outcome was exactly as he had imagined: "This isn't an owners' meeting, it's just a work report meeting."

Mimicking the way senior officials speak, Mr Mak described the proceedings as "unsatisfactory": "They couldn't deliver what we asked for, and they deleted the agenda items we requested — what do you think, is that satisfactory?" He was also unhappy: "They say everything has nothing to do with them, just like government officials talking — saying we can't do this, that's the government's job. But they're our representatives, aren't they? Shouldn't they be raising our demands with the government? All they do is say we can't do anything, what's the point of us?" Nevertheless, he said this was expected, noting that Hop On itself was appointed by the government.

Said there was heckling at the meeting: If this were a venue, there could have been a riot

Mr Mak criticised the first round of questions, noting that at the Tin Shui Wai venue only one person was allowed to ask questions: "So many people wanted to ask but couldn't, and the answers didn't address the questions." Residents in the audience heckled from time to time. "We've endured for seven months, bottled up our frustration for seven months — do you think we won't protest? If we were at one single venue, there could have been a riot," he said.

Mr and Mrs Mak were original residents of Wang Fuk Court. Believing the information was unclear, they have not yet submitted their acquisition intention letter: "We want to wait and see." They also frankly said that returning to live in Tai Po "is our dream," but for now there is "nothing to plan." They hope to be able to go back upstairs again to retrieve belongings, "take everything we can," noting that their home is still in good condition but they have so far only recovered less than a third of their belongings: "Only two sessions of six hours each, how much can you actually take?"

Elderly woman from Wang Tai Court chooses to sell her title: No choice, have to accept it

An elderly woman in her seventies living in Wang Tai Court also left at around 1:30 pm, saying: "Once I heard what I most wanted to hear, I left." She said her main concern was whether the remaining management fees and other sums for the estate would be returned to owners after selling their titles, and Hop On stated at the meeting that "we will return them to you." As for insurance compensation matters, she said: "If there's something to get, there is; if not, there isn't." She was not worried about being denied insurance payouts after selling her flat, joking: "I trust the government — the government shouldn't cheat us. Still picking food from a beggar's pocket? If it should be paid, pay it; if it shouldn't be collected, don't collect it."

The elderly woman currently lives in transitional housing in Hung Shui Kiu. She said her first choice was to attend in Tai Po and had planned to "meet up with friends for dim sum while I'm at it," but "couldn't get a slot so I came here instead." Nearly eight months since the fire, she said she initially felt "it was nothing much," but "the longer I live here, the more unhappy I become." "After all, you don't have your own home… the place is small, nothing compared to the old flat, at least two times worse, it feels like there's no activity space anywhere." She therefore hopes to go back upstairs as soon as possible.

Having moved in when Wang Fuk Court was first built, the elderly woman has signed the agreement to sell her title. Asked about giving up a home of more than 40 years, she said: "There's nothing I can do, I have to accept it," adding with a bitter smile: "If you don't sell, what then? If you absolutely refuse to sell, what good is holding onto the title? You have nowhere to live, so you have to be realistic about this."

Four tour buses and one minibus were parked at the scene to transport residents away, with assistance from a Care Team. The press area was set up more than ten metres from where residents boarded the buses, separated by railings.

Mr Yuen of Wang Shing Court: At least put on a show, bring out the reports

After the meeting, Wang Kin Court resident Mr Yuen told reporters he had no expectations for the meeting and ultimately got no answers: "They just repeated what they've said before." He said residents were most concerned about the investigation report and wanted to understand why all eight blocks had to be demolished: "Everyone wants to know why they lost their home, but no one can give an answer." Hop On also said it was "not their concern."

Regarding the investigation report, Hop On said there would be typhoon and rainy seasons ahead and they had to wait for authorities to check safety conditions: "Everyone wait a while, once they've done it they may announce it to everyone." This provoked heckling from several residents. Mr Yuen said, although everyone knew why they had to "take back the entire plot of land," "at the very least put on a show and bring out the reports, but they couldn't even produce them, saying typhoons and rain prevented them from getting the reports. Well, there's nothing we can do, we're just ordinary citizens, there's nothing more we can say."

Wang Kin Court resident Mr Yuen

Speaking about the meeting, Mr Yuen frankly said: "I don't have any feelings about it anymore, I expected it. I think sitting inside was just a process." He has not yet signed the intention letter, saying there are still many considerations, including how to handle things for his parents and children: "It's not like you sell it and the problem is solved." Nearly eight months since the fire, he said: "These eight months of suffering, I had to deal with it all myself… the whole family suffers, but we have to face it."

Asked if there was anything he wanted to say to the government or Hop On, Mr Yuen said calmly: "I think whatever we say is pointless, because they think they're doing a great job, that the arrangements are very well done. Whatever we say, people have already been saying it all along. Whether they like to hear it or not, I think we've already expressed ourselves. So… we should really thank them."

Ms Wong of Wang Chi Court

Wang Chi Court resident questions selling flat without knowing insurance compensation

Wang Chi Court resident Ms Wong said after the meeting she felt "very helpless and exhausted," explaining she had originally hoped to find out whether the HK$2 billion fire insurance would be paid out if the buildings were not rebuilt or repaired. A representative from Taiping Insurance said at the meeting: "If compensation is due, it will be paid," but the actual arrangements remain unclear and unresolved. She said the normal process should be to first calculate the compensation amount, then decide whether to sell, questioning whether, without knowing the insurance compensation, "we already have to sell our titles before 31 August — has the order been reversed?"

Ms Wong has not yet signed the acquisition intention letter, saying she has many questions and wants clear information before deciding. She hopes Hop On will reflect to the government the need to delay the deadline for selling flats, allowing residents to have more information about insurance compensation before deciding whether to sign the sale agreement. She also believes the next owners' meeting should be held as soon as possible, not after residents have sold their titles on 31 August. She stressed that Wang Chi Court was not burned and is completely safe: "Why can't I go back to my home?… What regulation, what department is stopping us from going home to get our things?" Residents asked the question several times at the meeting but got no answer.

Situation inside Tin Shui Wai venue (provided by owners on site)

Uncomfortable with the broadcast arrangements, making the process run poorly

Regarding the meeting arrangements, Ms Wong frankly said she was "very uncomfortable," explaining that at previous meetings all residents attended in person, but this time they were scattered across three venues, where attendees could "only stare at the screen" and couldn't even see what was happening at other venues. Whenever she wanted to ask a question or get the chairperson to clarify something, she had to rely on staff at the venue to relay the message, often without success. The process was also not smooth — they had to take turns drawing lots and asking questions, wasting considerable time, similar to the last briefing session. She believed that if residents could communicate and discuss in the same venue, the process would run more smoothly and require less manpower and resources, and she hopes Hop On can improve this next time.

Although dissatisfied with the meeting arrangements, Ms Wong described it as a joyful reunion with fellow residents and "being able to discuss things together," saying she felt a little comforted: "Finally the first meeting is being held. Although this meeting seems to have got few answers, seeing the neighbours, we can talk things through together."

Mr Tsang of Wang Yan Court

Mr Tsang of Wang Yan Court: Endless run-around, it's just a show

Mr Tsang, an owner who has lived in Wang Yan Court for a year and a half, described the entire meeting as "nothing more than a show" as he left. The agenda was set by Hop On and owners' questions went unanswered: "A lot of things just lead you around in circles." On the insurance issue in particular, he said residents were worried that after selling their titles, whether insurance would be paid to the government. The chairperson did not answer, "just kept running us around in circles."

Mr Tsang has no plans to sell his title for now. He said the government requires residents to sell their titles by 31 August or face legal action, but the insurance company says it will decide on compensation after the government issues its investigation report, while the government says the report can only come after the titles are sold: "Everyone pushes it back and forth, no decision can be made." He hopes the sale deadline can be delayed, or the report issued earlier.

Regarding the resolution at the meeting to hold another owners' meeting within two months, Mr Tsang is worried that if the next meeting is held after 31 August, the government will already hold most of the titles and be able to determine the direction and content of the meeting, leaving residents unable to have much say. He is also unhappy that residents have been "scattered" to different venues, making communication difficult, and believes the government is "very worried about us uniting."

Mr Li of Wang Tao Court fails authorisation, delayed over an hour before being allowed in

Mr Li of Wang Tao Court likewise felt that the meeting "couldn't really help with anything" and failed to answer owners' questions: "Everyone had so many uncertainties, and coming to this owners' meeting, it's still the same, so many things remain unknown." He said he felt that "after selling the title, there are many things you can no longer pursue," including insurance and the right to owners' meetings. He also believes that at the next meeting the government will already hold most of the titles, making attendance pointless.

Mr Li was authorised by a family member to attend, and originally submitted all the required documents before the deadline, but the day before the meeting he was notified that the authorisation had failed without any reason given. When he called the Hop On hotline, he got no answer. He returned to the venue at 10 am today, and staff again gave no reason for the failed authorisation, but checked his documents, and after going back and forth for an hour, finally allowed him into the venue at 11:15 am.

The Tin Shui Wai vote-monitoring lawyer did not reveal his name or law firm when pressed by residents, and did not respond to reporters' questions when leaving the hall.

Tin Shui Wai vote-monitoring lawyer refuses to identify himself

Additionally, lawyers were present to monitor the vote-counting at all venues. More than one resident mentioned that the lawyer at the Tin Shui Wai venue did not identify himself at the time, and only when pressed by residents did the host point out a particular man as the lawyer. However, he said he did not have a business card and refused to reveal his name or law firm. Residents pressed him about his identity, and Hop On said it would look into it, but in the end his identity was never confirmed. Wang Tai Court owner Mr Cheng described the situation as very strange, questioning whether "people are just putting on a show here, casually calling him a monitoring lawyer." The man walked out of the hall at around 5 pm, and when reporters asked if he was a lawyer, his name, and which firm he belonged to, he did not respond and immediately turned around and went back into the hall.
